source_batch.unit_label: CB Module E unit 3: development, regulation and supervision of co-operative banks (courseware unit 15)

facts.statement: Growth of the co-operative banking system and dual control (courseware): the agricultural credit system as it has emerged is a product of both evolution and intervention; the importance of rural credit received attention while enacting the Reserve Bank of India Act, 1935 following which the Agricultural Credit Department came into existence; Section 54 of the RBI Act authorised the creation of an Agricultural Credit Department within the Reserve Bank to deal with rural credit and long-term finance; Section 17 of the Act has empowered it to provide agricultural credit through state co-operative banks; the All-India Rural Credit Survey (1954) recommended the creation of the National Agricultural Credit Fund; the Agricultural Refinance Corporation (ARC) was set up by the Reserve Bank in 1963 for providing funds by way of refinance to institutions providing credit directly to the rural sector; renamed the Agricultural Refinance and Development Corporation (ARDC) in 1975; the Lead Bank Scheme was introduced to spearhead the decentralised credit planning; the Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) were set up in 1975 to resolve problems (co-operatives lacked resources); NABARD was set up on July 12, 1982 and took over the entire functions of the ARDC, the refinancing functions of the Reserve Bank in relation to co-operatives and RRBs. The State Government and the Registrar of Co-operative Societies appointed by the State are the main regulatory authorities for the co-operative societies that are operating only within a State; the regulation and supervision of the urban co-operative banks (UCBs) have been brought within the ambit of the Reserve Bank by the Banking Laws (Applicable to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1966 which came into force from March 1, 1966; as regards rural co-operative banks, the regulatory powers conferred on the Reserve Bank are limited; while the principle of supervision as regards primary agricultural credit societies and land development banks, the Act does not apply to the primary agricultural credit societies. Structure: an important feature of providing agricultural credit in India has been the existence of a widespread network of financial institutions; the present structure of the rural financial institutions consists of three-tier rural co-operative credit institutions, namely, the Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS), the district central co-operative banks (DCCBs), the State co-operative banks (SCBs); Regional Rural Banks (RRBs), Local area banks (LABs), urban co-operative banks (UCBs) and branches of commercial banks; the rural co-operative credit structure consists of many types of institutions; the number of various co-operative institutions at present is about 1,10,000; the share of co-operatives credit to agriculture has been declining with the share of commercial banks and RRBs increasing during the period 1975-76 to 2012-13 (courseware: the share of co-operatives declined from 28.7 per cent to 11.3 per cent while the share of RRBs moved up from 11.1 per cent to 11.9 per cent and commercial banks moved up considerably from 60.2 per cent to 76.8 per cent in 2019-20). Duality of control: the duality of control over the co-operative institutions is a contentious issue; the Task Force on Co-operative Credit Society System (Chairman: Jagdish Capoor, 1999) addressed the issue of duality of control over co-operative credit institutions and suggested the removal of overlap of controls to endow functional autonomy and operational freedom to co-operatives; the Task Force suggested drawing up of an Action Plan to redefine the roles and responsibilities and areas of regulation through delegation of powers in respect of all the players in the field, viz. the State Government, Reserve Bank, NABARD, and co-operative institutions; a system of preparation of institution specific development action plans and execution of Memorandum of Understanding have been initiated since 2003-04; a Task Force (Chairman: A. Vaidyanathan) was appointed in August 2004 to examine the issues relating to an appropriate regulatory framework for rural co-operative banking institutions; the recommendations of the Task Force have been accepted in principle by the Government.

Strengthening UCBs and the supervisory system (courseware): urban co-operative banks (UCBs): the Reserve Bank has undertaken a series of measures directed towards strengthening of the UCBs; since March 31, 1993, the UCBs have been brought within the ambit of the Reserve Bank prudential norms, which include the applicability of the capital adequacy standards, prescribing an asset-liability management framework, enhancing the proportion of holding of Government and other approved securities for the purpose of SLR stipulation, restriction on bank finance against the security of corporate shares and debentures, and limiting the exposure to capital market investment; the Reserve Bank appointed a High-Power Committee (Chairman: K. Madhava Rao, 1999) to review the performance of UCBs and to suggest necessary measures to strengthen the existing urban bank structure. Supervisory system: instances such as the Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank failure brought to fore the need for stringent regulatory control; the Reserve Bank extended the Off-site Surveillance System (OSS) to all non-scheduled UCBs having deposit size of Rs 100 crore and above; a supervisory reporting system was introduced for the scheduled UCBs since March 2001 as a first step towards setting up of OSS; the capital adequacy norms have been introduced in a phased manner since March 2002; better risk management through avoidance of concentration of credit risk, off-site surveillance for non-scheduled UCBs and KYC guidelines were introduced; a complete ban was imposed since October 2003 on grant of loans and advances to directors of UCBs, their relatives and concerns in which they have interest with a view to preventing certain irregularities; the Reserve Bank also directed that UCBs should undertake due diligence in respect of investments in non-SLR securities; the Reserve Bank introduced a new system of grading of UCBs in April 2003 which is based on their CRAR, level of net NPAs, record of losses and compliance with regulatory environment; similarly a system of supervisory rating for UCBs under the CAMELS model has also been introduced (initially implemented for scheduled UCBs but subsequently its simplified version was extended to non-scheduled UCBs in March 2004). Since the 1950s, the Reserve Bank has been striving to smoothen the process of flow of credit to the rural sector; the Reserve Bank brought out a Draft Vision Document (2005) for UCBs seeking to rationalise the existing regulatory and supervisory system, facilitate a focused system of supervision through enhancement of technology and evolve mechanism to address the issues arising out of dual control. Dual control and the amendment to the Banking Regulation Act, 1949: the Reserve Bank powers to regulate and supervise co-operative banks were limited due to non-applicability of certain statutory provisions of the BR Act, 1949 on co-operative banks, which affected its ability to take necessary and timely corrective actions in case of irregularities/weaknesses in functioning of these banks; the amendment to the BR Act, carried out in 2020 sought to protect the interests of depositors and strengthen co-operative banks by improving governance framework and oversight by the Reserve Bank, while enabling better access to capital; the amendment came into force for urban co-operative banks (UCBs) with retrospective effect from June 29, 2020, and for State Co-operative Banks (StCBs) and District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs) with effect from April 1, 2021. The amended Section 3 of the BR Act, 1949 makes the provisions of the Act inapplicable to Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS) or co-operative societies whose primary object and principal business is providing long-term finance for agricultural development, and so long as such societies do not use the words bank, banker or banking in their name and do not act as drawee of cheques; the amendment of Section 45 of the Act enabled the Reserve Bank to reconstruct or amalgamate a bank, with or without implementing a moratorium, with the approval of the Central Government; the amendment also provides the Reserve Bank powers to supersede the Board of Directors of a co-operative bank in consultation with the state government concerned; the amendment to Section 56 of the Act will help in narrowing down the regulatory arbitrage between commercial banks and co-operative banks. Amalgamation of co-operative banks: in the past, mergers and amalgamations between UCBs had to be approved by both the Reserve Bank and the respective Registrar of Co-operative Societies; following the enactment of the Banking Regulation (Amendment) Act, 2020, the Reserve Bank received greater powers for sanctioning the process of amalgamation; Master directions in this regard were issued on March 23, 2021 specifying the necessary conditions for voluntary amalgamation, including, inter alia, approval of the proposal by two-thirds of board members of the concerned UCB; the criterion for consideration of the proposal by the Reserve Bank is based on whether the amalgamated bank assures to protect deposits of the amalgamated bank either through its own resources or through financial support from the state government; incentives extended to the amalgamating bank include greater flexibility to close loss-making branches, open new branches, and retention of authorised dealer (AD) -I licence of the amalgamated bank; similarly the Reserve Bank on May 24, 2021 specified requirements and indicative benchmarks/conditions for voluntary amalgamation of DCCBs with StCBs.

Recent developments, agenda and the four-tier framework (courseware): the Reserve Bank continues to play a key role in strengthening the co-operative banking sector by fortifying the regulatory and supervisory framework. Goals set for 2020-21: refinement of the regulatory framework for co-operative banks; a discussion paper on strengthening the regulatory framework for capital adequacy in UCBs; a Supervisory Action Framework (SAF) for the state co-operative banks (StCBs) and district central co-operative banks (DCCBs); and faster resolution of weak UCBs which are under All-Inclusive Directions (AID). Implementation status: large number of UCBs are community/region-based which hinders the process of mergers and consolidation in the sector; an expert committee on UCBs set up in February 2021 examines the prospects of consolidation; the amendment in the BR Act (as applicable to co-operative societies - AACS) has brought in significant changes in the statutory provisions applicable on cooperative banks; the draft SAF for StCBs and DCCBs was at the stage of consultation with NABARD, the supervisor of these banks; speeding up the resolution of weak UCBs under AID is ongoing. Major developments: System-Based Asset Classification: to improve the efficiency, transparency and integrity of the asset classification process, UCBs with total assets of Rs 2,000 crore or above as on March 31, 2020, were advised to implement system-based asset classification with effect from June 30, 2021; UCBs with total assets of Rs 1,000 crore or above but less than Rs 2,000 crore which have self-assessed themselves as being at Level III or Level IV based on their digital depth and interconnectedness to the payment systems landscape in terms of the circular dated December 31, 2019, on Comprehensive Cyber Security Framework for UCBs were advised to implement the same from September 30, 2021. Submission of returns under Section 31 of the BR Act (AACS): time extended due to the Covid-19 pandemic. Interest Subvention Scheme for MSMEs: all cooperative banks were included as Eligible Lending Institutions under the Interest Subvention Scheme (ISS) for MSMEs 2018 of the Government of India with effect from March 3, 2020 (2 per cent subvention on outstanding fresh/incremental term loan/working capital limited to Rs 1 crore). Loans and advances to directors, relatives and firms/concerns (February 5, 2021): UCBs were advised not to make, provide or renew any loans and advances or extend any other financial accommodation to or on behalf of their directors or their relatives or to the firms/companies/concerns in which the directors or their relatives are interested (collectively called director-related loans); the directors or their relatives shall also not act as surety/guarantor. Voluntary amalgamation of UCBs: on March 23, 2021 the Reserve Bank issued Master Direction on voluntary amalgamation of UCBs under the provisions of Section 44A, read with Section 56 of the Banking Regulation (BR) Act, 1949 as amended vide BR (Amendment) Act, 2020. Agenda for 2021-22: setting up of an Umbrella Organisation (UO) for UCBs: National Urban Co-operative Finance and Development Corporation Ltd. was incorporated on April 18, 2020, as a non-government company under the Companies Act, 2013, having its registered office in New Delhi, with enrolment of UCBs as shareholder members; the UO is required to apply to the Reserve Bank for obtaining certificate of registration as NBFC. Revised regulatory framework: categorisation of UCBs for regulatory purposes: given the heterogeneity in the cooperative sector, the need for a tiered regulatory framework was felt; the Reserve Bank constituted the Expert Committee on UCBs and released the Revised Regulatory Framework for UCBs on July 19, 2022; accordingly the Reserve Bank decided to adopt a four-tiered regulatory framework, as against the existing two-tiered framework; detailed guidelines issued by notification dated 1 December 2022; the UCBs have been categorised into four tiers for regulatory purposes: Tier 1: all unit UCBs and salary earners UCBs (irrespective of deposit size), and all other UCBs having deposits up to Rs 100 crore; Tier 2: UCBs with deposits of more than Rs 100 crore and up to Rs 1,000 crore; Tier 3: UCBs with deposits more than Rs 1,000 crore and up to Rs 10,000 crore; Tier 4: UCBs with deposits more than Rs 10,000 crore; the deposits referred to above shall be reckoned as per audited balance sheet as on 31st March of the immediate preceding financial year; if a UCB transits to a higher Tier on account of increase in deposits in any year, it may be provided a glide path of up to a maximum of three years to comply with higher regulatory requirements. Net worth: Tier 1 UCBs operating in a single district shall have minimum net worth of Rs 2 crore; all other UCBs (of all tiers) shall have minimum net worth of Rs 5 crore; UCBs which currently do not meet the minimum net worth requirement shall achieve the minimum net worth of Rs 2 crore or Rs 5 crore (as applicable) in a phased manner: at least 50 per cent of the applicable minimum net worth on or before March 31, 2026 and the entire stipulated minimum net worth on or before March 31, 2028. CRAR: Tier 1 UCBs shall maintain, as hitherto, a minimum CRAR of 9 per cent of Risk Weighted Assets (RWAs) on an ongoing basis; Tier 2 to 4 UCBs shall maintain a minimum CRAR of 12 per cent of RWAs on an ongoing basis; UCBs in Tier 2 to 4, which do not currently meet the revised CRAR of 12 per cent of RWAs, shall achieve the same in a phased manner: at least 10 per cent by March 31, 2024, 11 per cent by March 31, 2025, and 12 per cent by March 31, 2026. Financially Sound and Well Managed (FSWM) criteria for UCBs (circular of 1 December 2022): (a) the CRAR shall be at least 1 percentage point above the minimum CRAR applicable to an UCB on the reference date; (b) net NPA of not more than 3 per cent; (c) net profit for at least three out of the preceding four years subject to its not having incurred a net loss in the immediate preceding year; (d) no default in the maintenance of CRR/SLR during the preceding financial year; (e) sound internal control system with at least two professional directors on the Board; (f) Core Banking Solution (CBS) fully implemented; and (g) no monetary penalty should have been imposed on the bank on account of violation of RBI directives/guidelines during the last two financial years.

payload.title: Growth of the co-operative credit system and the duality of control
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Rural credit institutions:** the **RBI Act 1935** created an **Agricultural Credit Department** (**Section 54**); **Section 17** lets the Bank lend to **state co-operative banks**. After the **All-India Rural Credit Survey (1954)** the Bank set up the **Agricultural Refinance Corporation (1963)** → **ARDC (1975)** → **NABARD (12 July 1982)**, which took over the refinancing functions for **co-operatives and RRBs**; **Regional Rural Banks (1975)** were created because **co-operatives lacked resources**.

**Structure:** a **three-tier rural co-operative structure**: **Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS)**, **District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs)**, **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs)**; plus **RRBs, LABs, UCBs** and **commercial bank branches**; about **1,10,000** co-operative institutions. The **share of co-operatives in agricultural credit has fallen** while **commercial banks and RRBs** rose.

**Dual control:** the **State Government and the Registrar of Co-operative Societies** regulate societies working only within the State; the **Banking Laws (Applicable to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1966** (in force from **1 March 1966**) brought **UCBs** under the **Reserve Bank's regulation and supervision**; its powers over **rural co-operative banks** were **limited** and the Act **does not apply to PACS**. Dual control is **contentious**: the **Capoor Task Force (1999)** urged **removal of overlap** and **functional autonomy**, an **Action Plan** and **Memoranda of Understanding** (from **2003-04**); the **Vaidyanathan Task Force (August 2004)** examined the regulatory framework for **rural co-operative banks**, and its recommendations were **accepted in principle**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Overlap between state and central regulators is the structural weakness of co-operative banking.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which Act were urban co-operative banks brought under Reserve Bank regulation, and from when?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Banking Laws (Applicable to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1966, from 1 March 1966.

payload.title: Strengthening UCBs and the supervisory system; the 2020 amendment and amalgamation
payload.core_explanation_md:
**Prudential norms for UCBs (from 31 March 1993):** **capital adequacy**, an **ALM framework**, more **SLR holdings in government securities**, **limits on loans against shares and debentures** and on **capital market exposure**. The **Madhava Rao High-Power Committee (1999)** reviewed UCBs.

**Supervision:** after the **Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank failure** the Reserve Bank extended **off-site surveillance** to **non-scheduled UCBs with deposits of Rs 100 crore or more**; **supervisory reporting for scheduled UCBs from March 2001**; **capital adequacy phased in from March 2002**; **KYC**; a **ban on loans to directors, their relatives and related concerns from October 2003**; **due diligence on non-SLR investments**; **grading of UCBs from April 2003** (based on **CRAR, net NPAs, losses and compliance**); **CAMELS supervisory rating** (simplified version for **non-scheduled UCBs from March 2004**). The **Draft Vision Document (2005)** sought to rationalise supervision and address **dual control**.

**BR Act amendment 2020:** it improves **governance and oversight** and gives **better access to capital**; effective **29 June 2020** (UCBs, retrospective) and **1 April 2021** (StCBs and DCCBs). **Section 3** exempts **PACS** and societies providing **long-term agricultural finance** (provided they do **not use 'bank', 'banker' or 'banking'** or act as **drawee of cheques**); **Section 45** lets the Reserve Bank **reconstruct or amalgamate** (with or without moratorium) with **Central Government approval**; the Reserve Bank may **supersede the board** (in consultation with the **State Government**); **Section 56** narrows **regulatory arbitrage** with commercial banks.

**Amalgamation:** the **Master Direction of 23 March 2021** (under **Section 44A read with Section 56**) lets UCBs merge voluntarily with **approval of two-thirds of board members**; the Reserve Bank checks whether the merged bank **protects deposits** from **own resources or State support**; incentives include **closing loss-making branches**, **opening branches** and **retaining the AD-I licence**; **24 May 2021** conditions for **DCCB-StCB** mergers.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: The 2020 amendment gave the Reserve Bank commercial-bank-style tools over co-operative banks.

self_check.prompt_text: What approval is needed for a voluntary amalgamation proposal of a UCB, among the Master Direction conditions?
self_check.expected_takeaway: Approval of the proposal by two-thirds of the board members of the concerned UCB (plus Reserve Bank sanction).

payload.title: Recent developments, the umbrella organisation and the four-tier framework for UCBs
payload.core_explanation_md:
**2020-21 goals:** refine the **regulatory framework**, a paper on **capital adequacy in UCBs**, a **Supervisory Action Framework (SAF)** for **StCBs and DCCBs** (**NABARD is their supervisor**), and quicker resolution of **weak UCBs placed under All-Inclusive Directions (AID)**. Consolidation is hindered because UCBs are **community or region based**; an **expert committee** (February 2021) studied it.

**Other measures:** **system-based asset classification** (UCBs with assets of **Rs 2,000 crore or more**: from **30 June 2021**; **Rs 1,000-2,000 crore and Level III/IV in cyber security self-assessment**: from **30 September 2021**); **all co-operative banks eligible** for the MSME **Interest Subvention Scheme 2018** (from **3 March 2020**); **ban on director-related loans** (**5 February 2021**); the **umbrella organisation (UO)** for UCBs, **National Urban Co-operative Finance and Development Corporation Ltd (incorporated 18 April 2020)**, to be an **NBFC**.

**Four-tier framework (released 19 July 2022; notified 1 December 2022):**

| Tier | UCBs |
| --- | --- |
| **Tier 1** | **Every unit UCB and salary earners' UCB**, and other UCBs with **deposits up to Rs 100 crore** |
| **Tier 2** | Deposits **above Rs 100 crore up to Rs 1,000 crore** |
| **Tier 3** | **Above Rs 1,000 crore up to Rs 10,000 crore** |
| **Tier 4** | **Above Rs 10,000 crore** |

Deposits are measured on the **audited balance sheet of 31 March** of the previous year; a bank moving up a tier gets a **glide path of up to three years**.

**Net worth:** **Rs 2 crore** for **Tier 1 UCBs in a single district**, **Rs 5 crore** for all others; shortfalls to reach **50 per cent by 31 March 2026** and **full by 31 March 2028**.

**CRAR:** **9 per cent** for **Tier 1**, **12 per cent** for **Tiers 2 to 4** (glide: **10 per cent by March 2024, 11 per cent by March 2025, 12 per cent by March 2026**).

**Financially Sound and Well Managed (FSWM) criteria:** (a) **CRAR at least 1 percentage point above the applicable minimum**; (b) **net NPA not above 3 per cent**; (c) **net profit in at least three of the preceding four years** and **no net loss in the last year**; (d) **no CRR/SLR default** in the previous year; (e) **sound internal control with at least two professional directors**; (f) **Core Banking Solution fully implemented**; (g) **no monetary penalty in the last two years**.
payload.expanded_explanation_md: Tiering matches regulatory demands to the size and complexity of each co-operative bank.

self_check.prompt_text: What minimum CRAR applies to Tier 2 to Tier 4 UCBs under the revised framework?
self_check.expected_takeaway: 12 per cent of risk weighted assets.

items.title: Growth of the co-operative credit system and the duality of control
items.core_explanation_md:
**Rural credit institutions:** the **RBI Act 1935** created an **Agricultural Credit Department** (**Section 54**); **Section 17** lets the Bank lend to **state co-operative banks**. After the **All-India Rural Credit Survey (1954)** the Bank set up the **Agricultural Refinance Corporation (1963)** → **ARDC (1975)** → **NABARD (12 July 1982)**, which took over the refinancing functions for **co-operatives and RRBs**; **Regional Rural Banks (1975)** were created because **co-operatives lacked resources**.

**Structure:** a **three-tier rural co-operative structure**: **Primary Agricultural Credit Societies (PACS)**, **District Central Co-operative Banks (DCCBs)**, **State Co-operative Banks (StCBs)**; plus **RRBs, LABs, UCBs** and **commercial bank branches**; about **1,10,000** co-operative institutions. The **share of co-operatives in agricultural credit has fallen** while **commercial banks and RRBs** rose.

**Dual control:** the **State Government and the Registrar of Co-operative Societies** regulate societies working only within the State; the **Banking Laws (Applicable to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1966** (in force from **1 March 1966**) brought **UCBs** under the **Reserve Bank's regulation and supervision**; its powers over **rural co-operative banks** were **limited** and the Act **does not apply to PACS**. Dual control is **contentious**: the **Capoor Task Force (1999)** urged **removal of overlap** and **functional autonomy**, an **Action Plan** and **Memoranda of Understanding** (from **2003-04**); the **Vaidyanathan Task Force (August 2004)** examined the regulatory framework for **rural co-operative banks**, and its recommendations were **accepted in principle**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Overlap between state and central regulators is the structural weakness of co-operative banking.

self_check.prompt_text: Under which Act were urban co-operative banks brought under Reserve Bank regulation, and from when?
self_check.expected_takeaway: The Banking Laws (Applicable to Co-operative Societies) Act, 1966, from 1 March 1966.

items.title: Strengthening UCBs and the supervisory system; the 2020 amendment and amalgamation
items.core_explanation_md:
**Prudential norms for UCBs (from 31 March 1993):** **capital adequacy**, an **ALM framework**, more **SLR holdings in government securities**, **limits on loans against shares and debentures** and on **capital market exposure**. The **Madhava Rao High-Power Committee (1999)** reviewed UCBs.

**Supervision:** after the **Madhavpura Mercantile Co-operative Bank failure** the Reserve Bank extended **off-site surveillance** to **non-scheduled UCBs with deposits of Rs 100 crore or more**; **supervisory reporting for scheduled UCBs from March 2001**; **capital adequacy phased in from March 2002**; **KYC**; a **ban on loans to directors, their relatives and related concerns from October 2003**; **due diligence on non-SLR investments**; **grading of UCBs from April 2003** (based on **CRAR, net NPAs, losses and compliance**); **CAMELS supervisory rating** (simplified version for **non-scheduled UCBs from March 2004**). The **Draft Vision Document (2005)** sought to rationalise supervision and address **dual control**.

**BR Act amendment 2020:** it improves **governance and oversight** and gives **better access to capital**; effective **29 June 2020** (UCBs, retrospective) and **1 April 2021** (StCBs and DCCBs). **Section 3** exempts **PACS** and societies providing **long-term agricultural finance** (provided they do **not use 'bank', 'banker' or 'banking'** or act as **drawee of cheques**); **Section 45** lets the Reserve Bank **reconstruct or amalgamate** (with or without moratorium) with **Central Government approval**; the Reserve Bank may **supersede the board** (in consultation with the **State Government**); **Section 56** narrows **regulatory arbitrage** with commercial banks.

**Amalgamation:** the **Master Direction of 23 March 2021** (under **Section 44A read with Section 56**) lets UCBs merge voluntarily with **approval of two-thirds of board members**; the Reserve Bank checks whether the merged bank **protects deposits** from **own resources or State support**; incentives include **closing loss-making branches**, **opening branches** and **retaining the AD-I licence**; **24 May 2021** conditions for **DCCB-StCB** mergers.
items.expanded_explanation_md: The 2020 amendment gave the Reserve Bank commercial-bank-style tools over co-operative banks.

self_check.expected_takeaway: Approval of the proposal by two-thirds of the board members of the concerned UCB (plus Reserve Bank sanction).

items.title: Recent developments, the umbrella organisation and the four-tier framework for UCBs
items.core_explanation_md:
**2020-21 goals:** refine the **regulatory framework**, a paper on **capital adequacy in UCBs**, a **Supervisory Action Framework (SAF)** for **StCBs and DCCBs** (**NABARD is their supervisor**), and quicker resolution of **weak UCBs placed under All-Inclusive Directions (AID)**. Consolidation is hindered because UCBs are **community or region based**; an **expert committee** (February 2021) studied it.

**Other measures:** **system-based asset classification** (UCBs with assets of **Rs 2,000 crore or more**: from **30 June 2021**; **Rs 1,000-2,000 crore and Level III/IV in cyber security self-assessment**: from **30 September 2021**); **all co-operative banks eligible** for the MSME **Interest Subvention Scheme 2018** (from **3 March 2020**); **ban on director-related loans** (**5 February 2021**); the **umbrella organisation (UO)** for UCBs, **National Urban Co-operative Finance and Development Corporation Ltd (incorporated 18 April 2020)**, to be an **NBFC**.

**Four-tier framework (released 19 July 2022; notified 1 December 2022):**

| Tier | UCBs |
| --- | --- |
| **Tier 1** | **Every unit UCB and salary earners' UCB**, and other UCBs with **deposits up to Rs 100 crore** |
| **Tier 2** | Deposits **above Rs 100 crore up to Rs 1,000 crore** |
| **Tier 3** | **Above Rs 1,000 crore up to Rs 10,000 crore** |
| **Tier 4** | **Above Rs 10,000 crore** |

Deposits are measured on the **audited balance sheet of 31 March** of the previous year; a bank moving up a tier gets a **glide path of up to three years**.

**Net worth:** **Rs 2 crore** for **Tier 1 UCBs in a single district**, **Rs 5 crore** for all others; shortfalls to reach **50 per cent by 31 March 2026** and **full by 31 March 2028**.

**CRAR:** **9 per cent** for **Tier 1**, **12 per cent** for **Tiers 2 to 4** (glide: **10 per cent by March 2024, 11 per cent by March 2025, 12 per cent by March 2026**).

**Financially Sound and Well Managed (FSWM) criteria:** (a) **CRAR at least 1 percentage point above the applicable minimum**; (b) **net NPA not above 3 per cent**; (c) **net profit in at least three of the preceding four years** and **no net loss in the last year**; (d) **no CRR/SLR default** in the previous year; (e) **sound internal control with at least two professional directors**; (f) **Core Banking Solution fully implemented**; (g) **no monetary penalty in the last two years**.
items.expanded_explanation_md: Tiering matches regulatory demands to the size and complexity of each co-operative bank.

self_check.expected_takeaway: 12 per cent of risk weighted assets.
